title: US SPR & Storage Watch
dek: US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and commercial crude stocks, SPR inventory, the 2026 exchange/refill mechanics, and Cushing.

claims.text: Status check on Oct 18: no DOE award announcement for the 17-million-barrel SPR exchange solicitation issued Oct 16 had been published, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed it. The round, FY27 SPR Oil Release No. 1, is still open, with proposals due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 21, 2026. The earlier 40-million-barrel round, FY26 SPR Oil Release No. 4, whose bids closed Oct 6, also still shows no award information on DOE's exchange archive, unlike the three earlier FY26 rounds. The award announcements are the next dated events on the ledger.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposals on Oct 16 for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), Reuters reported. The round is a portion of the pending 40 million barrels that form the last batch of the US 172-million-barrel commitment under the March IEA coordinated release of 400 million barrels. The US has released about 132.5 million barrels from the SPR since the war began. DOE has not published awards from the late September re-offer of the 40 million barrels, but Friday's 17-million-barrel figure implies about 23 million barrels were awarded in that round, Energy Aspects wrote in a note cited by Reuters.

Status check on Oct 16: no DOE award announcement for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange had been published since bids closed Oct 6, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed the Oct 10 emergency 4-million-barrel Hurricane Isaias exchange. The ledger therefore still stands at up to 44 million barrels committed for November and December delivery, with returns plus premium barrels due from 2027.

Status check on Oct 15: no DOE award announcement for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange had been published since bids closed Oct 6, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed the Oct 10 emergency 4-million-barrel Hurricane Isaias exchange. The ledger therefore still stands at up to 44 million barrels committed for November and December delivery, with returns plus premium barrels due from 2027.

Two SPR exchange threads are open at once and are tracked here as one ledger. The first is the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange under the IEA-coordinated release: bids closed October 6 and the award is still pending. The second is an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels authorized October 10 for Hurricane Isaias disruptions. Combined, up to 44 million barrels of reserve crude is committed to move into the Gulf market in November and December 2026, every barrel a loan due back with premium barrels starting in 2027.

DOE issued the request for proposals for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange, drawn from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on October 6 and deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026. Borrowers return the oil plus premium barrels.
The bid window for the 40-million-barrel exchange closed at 11 a.m. CT. As of October 12, DOE has not announced the award; the award announcement is the next dated event on this ledger.

DOE authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels, 2 million each to ExxonMobil and BP America, to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias. The borrowed crude plus premium barrels is to be returned in 2027; ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

Next on the ledger: awarded exchanges under the 40-million-barrel tranche deliver through November and December 2026. Returns begin in 2027, with exchange returns running through 2029; earlier phases returned an average premium of about 25 percent, which DOE says expands long-term reserve inventory at no taxpayer cost.

DOE's per-site grade table as of August 20, 2026 showed 101.8 million barrels of sweet and 192.3 million of sour (294.1 million total), or roughly 34.6% sweet and 65.4% sour. DOE defines sweet as sulfur content no greater than 0.5% by weight and sour as greater than 0.5% but less than 2.0%; DOE's stated design ratio is about 40% sweet to 60% sour, based on likely US refinery needs, especially on the Gulf Coast.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

claims.text: DOE reported the reserve at 284.9 million barrels as of September 11, split 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters). Against the August 20 DOE table, sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels and sour about 4.2 million over roughly three weeks, with sweet leaving slightly faster in absolute terms; the sweet share slipped to about 34.0%, drifting further from DOE's 40% design target. Note the September 11 split comes from secondary reporting of a DOE figure, not the published Quick Facts grade table.
claims.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

claims.text: The September 11 total sat about 32.5 million barrels above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates, so the exchange program has limited drawdown room left before hitting the statutory floor. DOE says it has secured cancellation of 140 million barrels of congressionally mandated sales scheduled for fiscal years 2024 through 2027, so there is no forced-sale overhang on the forward calendar.
claims.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine); US Department of Energy (energy.gov)

claims.text: EIA reported on Oct 15 that US commercial crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, against a Reuters poll expectation for a 288,000-barrel draw. Cushing stocks rose 1.9 million barrels, gasoline rose 3.5 million barrels to 208.3 million, distillate fell 2.5 million barrels to 102.6 million, and refinery utilization rose 0.8 points to 93.5 percent. The SPR was unchanged on the week at 283.0 million barrels.

API estimated US crude inventories fell 11.12 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, after a 2.09-million-barrel fall the prior week, while no barrels left the SPR that week, leaving the reserve at 283 million barrels, still 431 million below maximum capacity. API also put distillate stocks down 1.5 million barrels and gasoline up 1.1 million barrels; official EIA figures were due later on Oct 15.

Gulf of Mexico shut-ins fell sharply by Oct 12 to about 604,503 b/d of oil, 29.63 percent of current daily production, and 531 million cubic feet a day of gas, down from a peak near 1.46 million b/d ahead of Hurricane Isaias landfall, according to the federal offshore regulator's operator reports. Only five production platforms still had personnel evacuated. Shell reported no damage at its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets and was redeploying personnel, BP was restarting production at Na Kika and Thunder Horse, and Chevron was restoring full production after curbing five facilities.

Gulf of Mexico oil shut-ins eased to 57.54 percent (about 1.17 million b/d) by Oct 11, down from 62.89 percent on Oct 8, with personnel evacuated from 32 platforms, down sharply from 121 at the storm's peak, as operators began returning crews to undamaged facilities.

Chevron reported it kept production running at four of its nine Gulf platforms through Hurricane Isaias while five were temporarily shut in, and said crew remobilization would continue through Sunday under standard storm recovery procedures at its onshore facilities.

Hurricane Isaias shut in about 1.46 million b/d of Gulf of Mexico oil production with 129 platforms evacuated as the Category 3 storm made landfall late Oct 9 near the Alabama-Florida line; WTI settled at $91.85 and Brent at $104.72 to start the weekend, with the market weighing storm damage against the Hormuz tanker-attack risk.

The IEA agreed on Oct 15 to accelerate the release of the remaining volumes from its March 2026 collective action, including over 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible, its governing board said after meeting on Thursday. Members had pledged more than 400 million barrels in March. Analysts noted the diesel volume looks like an acceleration of existing commitments rather than new barrels, below the 50 million barrels of diesel discussed earlier in a French proposal.

Details of the Oct 9 Trump-Putin diesel deal now total 4.8 million tons: 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 in November, 1 million after that, and up to 3 million more depending on Russian refinery condition; US diesel futures fell almost 5% to about $4.64 a gallon on the news while AAA's national average sat near a record $6.28.

OFAC General License 135, signed minutes before Trump's Oct 9 announcement, authorizes the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel through 12:01 a.m. EDT on April 7, 2027, while barring debits to US accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund and Finance Ministry.

Trump said he would soon issue a directive under the Defense Production Act aimed at expanding US refining capacity; three industry sources told Reuters it could take the form of a presidential memo, as record diesel prices collide with the Iran war's strain on supply.

President Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, plus 500,000 tons in November, 1 million 'immediately thereafter' and 3 million more to follow; Treasury issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, and diesel futures dipped on Friday. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the refinery strikes.

Germany will release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, heating oil and crude from emergency reserves under the G7 plan, Economy Minister Katherina Reiche told Reuters on Friday, the largest European contribution so far; diesel and heating oil go first, with no product breakdown or timeline given.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Oct 8 that member countries still hold about 1.1 billion barrels of public emergency oil stocks, including over 200 million barrels of diesel, and stand ready to release more to the market if and when required.

In a televised national address on Oct 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu confirmed France will make 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves available to distributors at cost price over about three months (Nov 2026 to Jan 2027), projected to cut diesel prices at the pump by 12 to 18 euro cents per liter; he will sign a decree authorizing the operation.

Gasoline stocks rose 400,000 barrels (6% below the five-year average) while distillate stocks were essentially unchanged and sit 12% below the five-year average; four-week implied demand averaged 21.1 million b/d, up 0.7% year on year.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 16 that if companies take the full 17 million barrels in the new solicitation before any repayments arrive, SPR inventories would fall from about 283 million barrels to roughly 266 million, inside the 250 to 300 million barrel range generally considered the reserve's operational minimum zone. The June offer of the same final tranche drew agreement to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned.

The Oct 16 solicitation re-offers the remainder of the final SPR exchange tranche first offered in June, when companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned to the SPR, Reuters reported. Borrowers under an exchange return the crude plus premium barrels at a later date.

The DOE authorized an emergency SPR exchange of up to 4 million barrels (2 million each for ExxonMobil and BP America) to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias, with the borrowed crude plus premium barrels to be returned in 2027. ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

The bid window for DOE's sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange closed on Oct 6 at 11 a.m. CT, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026; the tranche completes the US portion of the 172-million-barrel pledge under the IEA-coordinated 400-million-barrel release, with borrowers returning the oil plus premium barrels.

The IEA said on Oct 3 that member countries have so far released about 325 million barrels of oil and oil products, more than 80% of the 400 million barrels pledged on March 11, the largest coordinated release in the agency's history. It remains unclear whether the G7's new 100-million-barrel release counts against the roughly 75 million barrels still outstanding under that pledge or comes on top of it.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposal on Sep 29 for an exchange of up to 40 million barrels of SPR crude from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026 and bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 6; DOE says five prior solicitations awarded more than 133 million barrels and earlier exchanges returned an average 25 percent premium.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright clarified in a CNBC interview that Venezuela's heavy crude would not be placed directly into reserve salt caverns but could be swapped for light or medium US barrels, because much of Venezuela's oil is heavier and higher in sulfur than the crude traditionally held in the reserve. Analysts quoted in the piece cautioned that many of the Venezuelan fields would need years of development and reinvestment before producing meaningful volumes.

In June 2026 the Department of Energy (DOE) awarded contracts for a further approximately 53.3 million barrels of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) exchange crude across all four sites (Bayou Choctaw, Bryan Mound, Big Hill, West Hackberry) under its late-April request for proposal, carrying an approximately 28 percent return premium (15.1 million barrels). DOE said about 35 million barrels had been delivered to market to that point and that earlier phases had awarded roughly 80 million barrels (45.2 plus 8.5 plus 26 million).

Other International Energy Agency (IEA) members' announced contributions to the 400-million-barrel coordinated release included 22.46 million barrels from South Korea and 13.5 million barrels from the United Kingdom, with Germany, Austria, and Japan also releasing stock (Japan's releases began in mid-March), per reporting in late July 2026. Aggregate member delivery progress beyond these pledges has not been published in a single authoritative ledger.

Federal law restricts non-emergency drawdowns once SPR inventories fall below 252.4 million barrels, and a 1981 GAO report advised against releases below 250 million except in a very severe emergency. With the reserve near 284 million barrels and another tranche now in motion, the legal floor is roughly 30 million barrels away.

DOE data released on Oct 13 put the SPR at 283 million barrels as of Oct 9, unchanged from the prior week and still the lowest since October 1982, about 13 million barrels above the first reading in August 1982. Senator Martin Heinrich raised concerns about salt cavern integrity at current low levels, while the administration said the caverns can be managed safely.

The SPR fell another 784,000 barrels to 283.0 million barrels, taking cumulative withdrawals since late March to 132.5 million barrels; combined commercial and SPR crude stocks drew 3.97 million barrels in the week.

Stocks of crude oil in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 283 million barrels in the week ending Oct 2, the lowest level since October 1982, according to Department of Energy data reported by Reuters. The drawdowns are part of the U.S. agreement to release 172 million barrels under the IEA coordinated action, and the administration last week offered to loan energy companies a further 40 million barrels from the reserve.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Oct 2, 2026; published Oct 5, 2026

claims.text: The Dallas Fed's third-quarter energy survey asked more than 100 oil and gas executives where the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) hits 'tank bottom,' the point at which oil can no longer be effectively recovered from the salt caverns. The largest share, 31%, put the practical minimum between 100 and 150 million barrels, 21% said 50 to 100 million, and 19% said 250 to 300 million, implying the reserve may already be near its operational floor. The survey puts the reserve at 283.7 million barrels at the end of September, 131.7 million below its pre-conflict level and its lowest since 1982.
Reuters reported US Strategic Petroleum Reserve stocks fell 800,000 barrels last week to 283.8 million barrels, the lowest level since October 1982, per Department of Energy data.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 25, 2026; published Sep 28, 2026

claims.text: OilPrice's weekly snapshot put the SPR at 283.8 million barrels after another 800,000 barrels left the reserve in the week ending Sep 25, against the reserve's roughly 714 million barrel design capacity.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 25, 2026; reported Sep 29, 2026

claims.text: The reserve held 284.6 million barrels in the week ending September 18, down 29.9 percent from a year earlier and down 130.5 million barrels since reaching 415.1 million on March 27, leaving it at roughly 40 percent of its 714-million-barrel design capacity across four Gulf Coast sites.
claims.vintage: Data: week ending Sep 18, 2026; published ~Sep 25, 2026; accessed 2026-09-28

claims.text: The Department of Energy's (DOE) Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) Quick Facts page put per-site inventory at 294.1 million barrels as of August 20, 2026: Bryan Mound 142.5 million (48 percent of the reserve), Big Hill 89.1 million, West Hackberry 30.5 million, and Bayou Choctaw 32.0 million. The quality split was 101.8 million barrels sweet and 192.3 million sour, meaning roughly 65 percent of the remaining reserve is sour crude.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

claims.text: The Department of Energy (DOE) lists the Strategic Petroleum Reserve's (SPR) maximum nominal drawdown capability at 4.4 million b/d with oil able to enter the market 13 days after a presidential decision, but effective capacity is lower: Big Hill's drawdown capability is currently zero because of a construction outage and West Hackberry is limited to 0.75 million b/d by low inventory.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts); Wikipedia (citing DOE facility data)

claims.text: From about 415 million barrels when the exchanges began in mid-March to 284.6 million in the week ending September 18, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) drew roughly 130 million barrels in about 27 weeks, an average pace of roughly 0.7 million b/d (Heavy Reading calculation from Department of Energy (DOE) and Energy Information Administration (EIA) figures).
claims.source: Heavy Reading calculation (DOE via TS2.Tech; EIA via Energy Factbook)

claims.text: The Senate-passed July 2025 budget bill cut Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) crude purchase funding to $171 million from the House's $1.3 billion, enough for roughly 3 million barrels instead of about 20 million at prevailing prices, according to Rapidan Energy cited in the reporting; the same bill kept the repeal of the last 7 million barrels of congressionally mandated SPR sales through fiscal year 2027 (Reuters).
